newsitem.title: MEXICO: Former ETA members live peacefully in Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Former ETA members live peacefully in Mexico.

text.p: Former members of Spain's outlawed Basque separatist rebels are living peacefully in Mexico but fear the government could bow to pressure from Spain to extradite them, a former ETA member said.
The killing of a young politician by members of Euzkadi Ta Askatasuna (Basque Homeland and Freedom) in Spain earlier this month unleashed outrage that spread to its former colony Mexico.
The issue flared this week, when Spanish newspaper ABC published a list of at least 75 alleged ETA members it claimed were living here.

Officials here deny that Mexico is knowingly sheltering ETA members. But one former member of the separatist group told Reuters ex-ETA members were living here, though he insisted all were peaceful citizens.

"All of us will have to face public opinion to make it known that we are not bandits and that we live in this country in a dignified manner," Luis Miguel Ipina, 46, told Reuters in an interview late on Tuesday at his modest house in the north of Mexico City.
Mexican officials on Wednesday said they were not launching an investigation into presumed ex-ETA members living in Mexico, but said they planned to cooperate with Spain.

"We cannot do anything on the basis of a list that is published or supposedly exists....but we are totally willing to cooperate with Spain as they have been with us, but within the law," Attorney General Jorge Madrazo told reporters.

Mexican Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria said on Tuesday that Mexico was not aware of a list of former ETA members living here, but conceded that some Spaniards here may have formerly belonged to the group and committed crimes in Spain.

"We have repeated that there does not exist any list of people in Mexico who are identified by the fact of their belonging or not to any particular organisation," Foreign Minister Jose Angel Gurria told reporters on Tuesday.
But if Madrid requested the extradition of any of these people, Mexico would proceed according to the law, he added.
Ipina said he feared this official position meant Mexico might bend to pressure from Spain's government.
In the living room of his small home decorated with an enormous Basque flag, Ipina told Reuters that he had left Spain for France and Guatemala before reaching Mexico.
Originally from San Sebastian, on Spain's north coast, he became a Mexican national after marrying a local woman. He now drives a taxi in the capital.
As an ETA member he handled weapons, prepared explosives, trained comrades and even took part in some attacks, he said.
He described the excitement of belonging to ETA 17 years after having left it, and challenged the Spanish government to publicly debate its reasons for rejecting Basque separatism.

"It would be a debate about independence," he said, adding this would help the public understand the reasons for the Basque independence struggle -- which he said was currently undergoing its severest repression since the time of former dictator General Francisco Franco, who governed Spain until his death in 1975.

He also denied accusations by some Spanish officials linking former ETA members in Mexico with Mexico's own home-grown brand of rebels -- the Zapatistas (EZLN) in the impoverished south and the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR) in the southwest.
"We are respectful of this country and we have no links with the EZLN or with the EPR," he said.
